hints: Remember that second ionisation starts not from a neutral atom but from the ion already formed after the first electron is lost.
walkthrough:
Picture what second means**
Think of ionisation as peeling electrons off one at a time. First ionisation removes one electron from neutral $\text{Ar}(\text{g})$ to give $\text{Ar}^{+}(\text{g})$. Second ionisation must therefore start from that $\text{Ar}^{+}(\text{g})$ ion.

Build the equation correctly**
Write the reactant as $\text{Ar}^{+}(\text{g})$. Remove one more electron to give $\text{Ar}^{2+}(\text{g}) + \text{e}^{-}$. Keep all species gaseous and balance charge: $+1$ on the left, $+2 + (-1) = +1$ on the right.
Final answer: $\text{Ar}^{+}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ar}^{2+}(\text{g}) + \text{e}^{-}$

hints: Write the electronic configuration of Ar (18 electrons) and count how many electrons are in the outer n = 3 shell.

Decide after which removal the next electron must come from the inner n = 2 shell, causing a large jump, and how this fixes the positions of the 8th and 9th points relative to the 7th and 10th points.
walkthrough:
Count the outer electrons**
Argon is $1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{6}$. The outer shell (n = 3) holds $2 + 6 = 8$ electrons. So removals 1 to 8 all come from the same shell at a similar distance with gradually increasing nuclear attraction.

Place the 8th point on the trend**
Look at the graph: points 1 to 7 rise gently from about $1500$ to about $12000$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. The 8th electron is the last n = 3 electron, so it continues that gentle rise. Place a cross at x = 8 a little above the 7th value, roughly $13000$ to $20000$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Spot the shell change for the 9th point**
The 9th electron must be removed from the n = 2 shell, much closer to the nucleus with less shielding. That needs much more energy, so there is a large jump between 8 and 9. Place a cross at x = 9 well above the 8th value but below the given 10th value at about $46000$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, roughly $35000$ to $45000$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: Plot cross at x = 8 in range 13000 to 20000 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ continuing the gradual rise.
Plot cross at x = 9 in range 35000 to 45000 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, showing a large jump before the given 10th value.

hints: Decide whether the first electron removed from Ar comes from a 3s or 3p orbital, then recall the characteristic shape of that orbital type.
walkthrough:
Identify which orbital loses the electron**
Argon ends in $3p^{6}$. The highest energy electrons are the $3p$ electrons, so the first ionisation removes a $3p$ electron.

Recall the p shape**
An s-orbital is spherical, but a p-orbital is a dumbbell. Draw two touching lobes meeting at a point (the nucleus), like a vertical figure of eight. Shading is not required, just the clear two lobe outline.
Final answer: Sketch a dumbbell / figure of eight shape with two lobes meeting at the nucleus (p-orbital).

hints: List p, V and T and convert them to SI units for the gas equation: kPa to Pa, $\text{cm}^{3}$ to $\text{m}^{3}$, and $^{\circ}\text{C}$ to K.
Recall the governing equation $pV = nRT$ rearranged to $n = pV/RT$ to find moles of $\text{Cl}_{2}$.
Convert moles to mass using mass = moles x $M_{r}$, with $M_{r}$ of $\text{Cl}_{2} = 71.0$.
walkthrough:
Convert everything to SI units**
You can only use $pV = nRT$ if units match $R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$. So convert: $$p = 404 \text{ kPa} = 404000 \text{ Pa}$$ $$V = 20.0 \text{ cm}^{3} = 20.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^{3}$$ $$T = 25^{\circ}\text{C} + 273 = 298 \text{ K}$$ A common slip is leaving volume in $\text{cm}^{3}$. That gives an answer a million times too big.

Find moles of chlorine**
Rearrange to $n = pV/RT$ and substitute: $$n = \dfrac{404000 \times 20.0 \times 10^{-6}}{8.31 \times 298} = 3.26 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol of Cl}_{2}$$ Keep extra figures for the next step.

Change moles to grams**
Each $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecule has mass $2 \times 35.5 = 71.0$. Use $m = n \times M$: $$m = 3.26 \times 10^{-3} \times 71.0 = 0.23 \text{ g}$$ Give 2 or 3 significant figures with unit g.

Final answer: $p = 404000 \text{ Pa}$, $V = 20.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^{3}$, $T = 298 \text{ K}$
$n = \dfrac{pV}{RT} = \dfrac{404000 \times 20.0 \times 10^{-6}}{8.31 \times 298} = 3.26 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
$\text{mass of Cl}_{2} = 3.26 \times 10^{-3} \times 71.0 = 0.23 \text{ g}$ (2 s.f.)

hints: Remember that one $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecule contains two Cl atoms, so first double the moles of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ to get moles of Cl atoms.
Recall how to change moles of atoms into number of atoms using the Avogadro constant, $6.02 \times 10^{23}$.
walkthrough:
Double for the diatomic molecule**
Your answer in (d)(i) is moles of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecules. Each molecule gives two separate Cl atoms: $$\text{mol Cl atoms} = 3.26 \times 10^{-3} \times 2 = 6.53 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ Forgetting this factor of 2 is the classic error here.

Multiply by Avogadro**
One mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles. So: $$\text{number} = 6.53 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 3.93 \times 10^{21} \text{ atoms}$$ If you used $0.36$ g as instructed, moles $\text{Cl}_{2} = 0.36/71.0$, giving about $6.11 \times 10^{21}$ atoms by the same method.

Final answer: $\text{moles of Cl atoms} = 3.26 \times 10^{-3} \times 2 = 6.53 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$
$\text{number of Cl atoms} = 6.53 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 3.93 \times 10^{21}$

hints: Recall the two main ideal gas assumptions: particles have negligible volume and have no intermolecular forces with elastic collisions.
Think about what squeezing particles very close together does to the volume assumption, and what removing kinetic energy at very low temperature does to attractions between particles.
walkthrough:
Start from the ideal model**
An ideal gas assumes two things: the particles themselves occupy zero volume, and there are no attractions between them so all collisions are perfectly elastic. Real $\text{Cl}_{2}$ only approximates this at moderate pressure and temperature.

Explain high pressure**
At very high pressure the gas is squeezed into a tiny volume. The $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecules are now close together, so the space they occupy is no longer negligible compared to the whole container. The free space available is less than the ideal equation assumes.

Explain low temperature**
At very low temperature particles move slowly with little kinetic energy. They cannot overcome the London dispersion forces between $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecules, so attractions become significant and collisions are no longer elastic. The gas is closer to liquefying, which the ideal model does not allow.

Final answer: At very high pressures: volume of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ molecules becomes significant / non-negligible compared to the container volume.
At very low temperatures: intermolecular forces become significant / collisions are no longer elastic as particles have insufficient kinetic energy to overcome attractions.
